summary.text: For primes \(p,q\) with different final digits and \(pq\le150\), if neither divides \(d\), then solving \(a+id\equiv0\pmod{pq}\) produces an index \(0\le i<150\) whose term has prime divisors with two different final digits; hence \(p\mid d\) or \(q\mid d\). Applying this to selected prime pairs and using \(d\le2025\) successively forces \(2,3,5,7,11\mid d\), so \(2310\mid d\), contradicting the bound.

full_proof.text:
We prove that no such arithmetic progression exists.

Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same last decimal digit. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025
\]
such that every one of the 150 integers
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
is lopsided.

We first establish the key obstruction.

**Lemma.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be primes whose last decimal digits are different, and suppose that \(pq\le 150\). Then
\[
p\mid d\quad\text{or}\quad q\mid d.
\]

**Proof of the lemma.** Suppose instead that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Since \(p\) and \(q\) have different last digits, they are distinct primes. It follows that \(d\) is relatively prime to both \(p\) and \(q\), and hence
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Therefore multiplication by \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). Consequently the congruence
\[
a+id\equiv 0\pmod{pq}
\]
has a solution modulo \(pq\), namely \(i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq}\). Choose its unique representative satisfying
\[
0\le i<pq.
\]
Because \(pq\le 150\), this representative satisfies \(0\le i<150\), so \(a+id\) is one of the assumed 150 lopsided terms.

On the other hand, \(pq\mid a+id\), so both primes \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). This term is positive because \(a\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), and \(i\ge0\). Thus \(p\) and \(q\) are prime divisors of this term, but their last decimal digits differ. Hence the term is not lopsided, a contradiction. This proves the lemma.

We now apply the lemma repeatedly. We will also use the elementary fact that if two relatively prime integers both divide \(d\), then their product divides \(d\). All products below are products of distinct primes, so this fact can be applied successively.

### Step 1: \(2\mid d\)

Apply the lemma to the five pairs
\[
(2,3),\ (2,5),\ (2,7),\ (2,11),\ (2,13).
\]
In each pair, the primes have different final digits: the final digit of \(2\) is \(2\), whereas those of \(3,5,7,11,13\) are respectively \(3,5,7,1,3\). Also every corresponding product is at most \(150\):
\[
2\cdot3=6,
\quad2\cdot5=10,
\quad2\cdot7=14,
\quad2\cdot11=22,
\quad2\cdot13=26.
\]
Thus the lemma gives
\[
2\mid d\text{ or }3\mid d,
\]
\[
2\mid d\text{ or }5\mid d,
\]
\[
2\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d,
\]
\[
2\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d,
\]
\[
2\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d.
\]
If \(2\nmid d\), all the other alternatives must hold, so
\[
3,5,7,11,13\mid d.
\]
These are distinct primes, and therefore their product divides \(d\):
\[
3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=15015\mid d.
\]
Since \(d\ge1\), this would imply \(d\ge15015\), contradicting \(d\le2025\). Therefore
\[
2\mid d.
\]

### Step 2: \(3\mid d\)

Apply the lemma to
\[
(3,5),\ (3,7),\ (3,11),\ (3,17).
\]
Their last digits are respectively \((3,5),(3,7),(3,1),(3,7)\), so they differ in every pair, and
\[
3\cdot5=15,
\quad3\cdot7=21,
\quad3\cdot11=33,
\quad3\cdot17=51,
\]
all of which are at most \(150\). Hence
\[
3\mid d\text{ or }5\mid d,
\]
\[
3\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d,
\]
\[
3\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d,
\]
\[
3\mid d\text{ or }17\mid d.
\]
If \(3\nmid d\), these imply that \(5,7,11,17\) all divide \(d\). From Step 1, \(2\mid d\) as well. The five primes are distinct, so
\[
2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090\mid d.
\]
This forces \(d\ge13090>2025\), a contradiction. Thus
\[
3\mid d.
\]

### Step 3: \(5\mid d\)

Apply the lemma to
\[
(5,7),\ (5,11),\ (5,13).
\]
Their last digits differ, and their products are
\[
5\cdot7=35,
\quad5\cdot11=55,
\quad5\cdot13=65,
\]
all at most \(150\). Therefore
\[
5\mid d\text{ or }7\mid d,
\]
\[
5\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d,
\]
\[
5\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d.
\]
If \(5\nmid d\), then \(7,11,13\mid d\). Steps 1 and 2 also give \(2,3\mid d\). Hence
\[
2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=6006\mid d.
\]
This gives \(d\ge6006>2025\), again impossible. Therefore
\[
5\mid d.
\]

### Step 4: \(7\mid d\)

Apply the lemma to
\[
(7,11),\ (7,13).
\]
The last digits are \((7,1)\) and \((7,3)\), and
\[
7\cdot11=77\le150,
\qquad
7\cdot13=91\le150.
\]
Thus
\[
7\mid d\text{ or }11\mid d,
\qquad
7\mid d\text{ or }13\mid d.
\]
If \(7\nmid d\), it follows that \(11,13\mid d\). Together with the already established divisibilities \(2,3,5\mid d\), this yields
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290\mid d.
\]
Thus \(d\ge4290>2025\), a contradiction. Hence
\[
7\mid d.
\]

### Step 5: \(11\mid d\)

Finally apply the lemma to \((11,13)\). These primes end in \(1\) and \(3\), respectively, and
\[
11\cdot13=143\le150.
\]
Therefore
\[
11\mid d\quad\text{or}\quad13\mid d.
\]
If \(11\nmid d\), then \(13\mid d\). By the preceding steps, \(2,3,5,7\mid d\) as well. Consequently
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730\mid d.
\]
This would imply \(d\ge2730>2025\), which is impossible. We conclude that
\[
11\mid d.
\]

We have now proved that each of the five distinct primes
\[
2,3,5,7,11
\]
divides \(d\). Their product therefore divides \(d\):
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310\mid d.
\]
Because \(d\) is positive, this implies
\[
d\ge2310.
\]
But the assumed bound is \(d\le2025\), and \(2310>2025\). This final contradiction proves that there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all 150 terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), have all their prime divisors ending in the same decimal digit. Thus the stated existence conjecture is false.
